definitions.definition: Ten goddesses who are forms of the one Goddess: Kālī, Tārā, Ṣoḍaśī (Tripurasundarī), Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī and Kamalā (Muṇḍamālā as quoted in the Tantrasāra); each has her Bhairava consort (Toḍala 1.3-19) and they correspond to Viṣṇu's ten avatāras (Toḍala 10.9-11). The lists differ: the Bṛhaddharma names Sundarī and Ṣoḍaśī separately and omits Kamalā.

Satī's ten forms, stationed in the ten directions around Śiva before she goes to Dakṣa's sacrifice; they grant liberation to worshippers and accomplish the magical acts (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.125-134; Mahābhāgavata 8).

relations.note: their origin in the Satī myth

name: Kālī (first Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Dark, naked, four-armed — sword and freshly severed head in the left hands, fear-dispelling and boon-giving gestures in the right — with a garland of heads, a girdle of hands, loose hair, lolling tongue and three eyes, standing on Śiva as a corpse in the cremation ground (Kālī Tantra dhyāna in the Tantrasāra). Teaching: she devours Time (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32); without her Śiva is a corpse (Toḍala 1.25); in the Toḍala she became Kṛṣṇa (10.11).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Tārā (second Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Blue-black, short and pot-bellied, standing in the archer's stance on a corpse, wearing a tiger skin and a garland of heads, with a single tawny braid (ekajaṭā) bearing Akṣobhya; in her four hands sword and cleaver, skull-cup and blue lotus (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: she who ferries across (tāraṇa) and goddess of speech (Nīlasarasvatī); Akṣobhya is her Bhairava because he drank the ocean's poison unagitated (Toḍala 1.4-6); linked with Mahācīna, Vasiṣṭha and the Buddha (Rudrayāmala 17; Tārā Tantra 1).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Ṣoḍaśī / Tripurasundarī (third Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Red, a sixteen-year-old, holding noose, goad, sugarcane bow and five flower arrows, seated on Sadāśiva on a couch whose legs are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: supreme beauty and bliss; with the five-faced Śiva as her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.7-8); her full cult is Śrīvidyā (U23).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Bhuvaneśvarī (fourth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Radiant as the rising sun, three-eyed, crowned with the crescent, holding noose and goad and showing boon and fearlessness (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: queen of the worlds and of space; Tryambaka is her Bhairava because he delights in her in heaven, earth and the underworld (Toḍala 1.9-10); in the Devī Gītā the supreme Goddess appears as Bhuvaneśvarī.

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Bhairavī / Tripurabhairavī (fifth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Red as a thousand rising suns, wearing a garland of heads, holding rosary and book (or noose and goad) and showing fearlessness and boon (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: the fierce power of dissolution and austerity; Dakṣiṇāmūrti is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.11); in the Bṛhaddharma Satī herself is Bhairavī within Śiva's body.

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Chinnamastā (sixth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Self-decapitated, holding her own head and a cleaver, three streams of blood rising from her neck — one into her own mouth and two into those of her attendants Ḍākinī and Varṇinī — standing on the god of love and his wife in union (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: Kabandha ('the headless') is her Bhairava, by whose worship one becomes lord of all powers (Toḍala 1.12-13). A Bengali account (Prāṇatoṣiṇī, citing earlier texts) tells that she cut off her own head to feed her hungry attendants.

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Dhūmāvatī (seventh Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: An old, smoky, dishevelled widow in a chariot bannered with a crow, holding a winnowing basket, hungry and quarrelsome (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: she has no Bhairava because she bears the form of a widow (Toḍala 1.13); worshipped to remove enemies and misfortune.

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Bagalāmukhī / Pītāmbarā (eighth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Golden-yellow, in yellow garments, seizing an enemy's tongue with her left hand and raising a club with her right, on a throne amid an ocean (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: the power of paralysing (stambhana) enemies and speech; the one-faced Mahārudra, destroyer of the world, is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.14).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Mātaṅgī (ninth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Dark green, playing the vīṇā, with a parrot (standard dhyāna, recalled); as Ucchiṣṭa-Mātaṅgī she receives leftover food. Teaching: goddess of speech, music and learning, a 'tantric Sarasvatī'; Mataṅga (Dakṣiṇāmūrti, 'joy of the world') is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.15).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Kamalā / Kamalātmikā (tenth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Golden, seated on a lotus, bathed by four elephants pouring nectar from jars, holding lotuses and showing boon and fearlessness (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: a tantric Lakṣmī of prosperity and grace; Sadāśiva in Viṣṇu's form is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.16).

members: Bhairava: Sadāśiva in the form of Viṣṇu
avatāra (Toḍala 10): — (the Toḍala assigns Buddha to Mahālakṣmī)
notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: The origin of the ten Mahāvidyās in the Satī–Śiva story

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: Satī wishes to attend her father Dakṣa's sacrifice, to which Śiva was not invited; when Śiva refuses, she turns dark and terrible and fills the ten directions with ten forms, the Mahāvidyās; she explains that she is the root Nature who took birth to win him, and goes (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.78-134; Mahābhāgavata 8). Her death at the sacrifice leads to the scattering of her body and the pīṭhas (Kālikā Purāṇa 18).

name: The Bhairava consorts of the Mahāvidyās

definitions.definition: Each Mahāvidyā is worshipped with her Bhairava at her right: Mahākāla (Dakṣiṇakālī), Akṣobhya (Tārā), five-faced Śiva (Tripurasundarī), Tryambaka (Bhuvaneśvarī), Dakṣiṇāmūrti (Bhairavī), Kabandha (Chinnamastā), none for the widow Dhūmāvatī, Mahārudra (Bagalā), Mataṅga (Mātaṅgī), Sadāśiva as Viṣṇu (Kamalā) (Toḍala 1.3-19).

name: The Mahāvidyās as the ten avatāras

definitions.definition: Toḍala 10.9-11 identifies the Mahāvidyās with Viṣṇu's avatāras — Tārā the Fish, Bagalā the Tortoise, Dhūmāvatī the Boar, Chinnamastā Nṛsiṃha, Bhuvaneśvarī Vāmana, Mātaṅgī Rāma, Tripurā Paraśurāma, Bhairavī Balabhadra, Mahālakṣmī the Buddha, Durgā Kalki, Kālī Kṛṣṇa — and promises equality with Mahādeva to their worshipper.

relations.standpoint: Śākta (the Goddess as source of the avatāras)
relations.note: Vaiṣṇava traditions reject the subordination of the avatāras to the Goddess

name: Kālī as Time and the devourer of Time

definitions.definition: Mahākāla devours all beings; Kālī devours Mahākāla and is therefore the primordial Kālikā (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32); she is 'mother of Time' (5.140) and witnesses Time at play (13.12); in the Krama she is the power of kalana in twelve phases (U19).

relations.note: Kashmirian Krama analysis of the same power

name: Kālī standing on Śiva as a corpse

definitions.definition: When Kālī manifests as dissolution Sadāśiva becomes a corpse: with Śakti he is Śiva, without her a corpse (śava), though he remains the Person (Toḍala 1.20-25); the Kālī Tantra's meditation places her on the heart of Mahādeva in corpse form (Tantrasāra).

Her form is imagined according to her qualities: black because all colours — all beings — vanish into her; the crescent for immortality; three eyes as moon, sun and fire; boon and fearlessness to protect; seated on a red lotus as ruling the worlds of rajas; pure consciousness watching Time play (Mahānirvāṇa 13.5-13; 5.140).
The devotional songs question and affirm her blackness: black to the world, she lights the lotus of the heart (Kamalākānta).

Four-armed, terrible-faced, with loose hair and garland of heads, sword and severed head in the left hands, fearlessness and boon in the right, on Śiva as a corpse, united with Mahākāla, smiling (Kālī Tantra as quoted in Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra); the Karpūrādistotra gives the same hands (v. 4). Bengali legend ascribes the fixing of this form to Kṛṣṇānanda.

name: Kālī as the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva

definitions.definition: As trees rise from the earth and bubbles from water, Brahmā and the gods are born from Kālikā and dissolve into her (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.42-43); she gives birth, protects and dissolves, and so is Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśa (Karpūrādistotra 12-14).

Kālī dwells in the cremation ground with jackals around her (Kālī Tantra dhyāna); the vīra worships her there at night (Karpūrādistotra, restricted); corpse and skull seats (śava-sādhana, pañcamuṇḍī) belong to the same setting (restricted, summary only). In Bengali devotion the heart is made the cremation ground so that the Mother may dance there (song ascribed to Rāmprasād, low confidence).

name: The Goddess's gentle and fierce forms

definitions.definition: The one Goddess appears as gentle (saumya: Kamalā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī) and fierce (ugra: Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī) forms; the forms are imagined according to her qualities and acts for the benefit of worshippers (Mahānirvāṇa 5.140; 13.13); Satī turns dark and fearsome to show Śiva her Mahāvidyā forms (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.78-80); Dakṣiṇakālī is terrible yet smiling and boon-giving (Tantrasāra).

Meditation on the Goddess is of two kinds; the formless is beyond speech and mind and reachable only by yogins through great effort; a form is imagined for the formless Kālī to steady the mind and awaken subtle meditation (Mahānirvāṇa 5.137-140); the formless Goddess produces form for the sake of worship (Nirvāṇa Tantra 1.2-5).
Nothing is without Bhairava and nothing without the Goddess; by cause and effect each is the other's guru (Kubjikāmata 2.17-18).
Without Śakti Śiva is a corpse (Toḍala 1.25).
Kula is Śakti and Akula Śiva; the Kaula joins them (Kulārṇava 17.27); their union is the bliss that is liberation (5.79).
The Goddess is the supreme power of knowledge, will and action, and the power of sound (Kubjikāmata 2.2).
Kālī is pure consciousness (cinmayī), witness of all (Mahānirvāṇa 13.12); she is the power without which Śiva is inert (Toḍala 1.25).
The root Nature, who as vidyā commands the three gods to create, protect and dissolve (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.98-124).

Countless universes made of the five elements rest like sand-grains on Ananta upon the cosmic tortoise in the ocean of compassion (Nirvāṇa Tantra 1.6-9); the gods arise from Kālī and dissolve into her (10.42-43).
The root Nature divides the Person into jīva and the supreme and herself into māyā and vidyā; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva receive their functions from her (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.98-124).

name: Tantra as the scripture of the Kali age

definitions.definition: In the Kali age only the Āgama's path avails; Vedic mantras are like snakes without poison (Mahānirvāṇa 2.7-15); only householder and mendicant stages remain (8.8); for the Kālīvilāsa only the paśu disposition remains and puraścaraṇa gives way to mental remembrance of the mantra (4.2-6).

name: Worship of Brahman in the Mahānirvāṇa

definitions.definition: Brahman is pure being beyond speech and mind, known in samādhi by those who see equally (Mahānirvāṇa 3.7-8), worshipped with the mantra 'oṃ saccidekaṃ brahma'; 'all is Brahman' is the attitude of the Tattva circle (8.208).
Akula is Śiva, Kula is Śakti; the Kaulas are adept in joining them (Kulārṇava 17.27); for Kaulas 'the non-Kula becomes Kula' (9.62).

Śiva as the supreme Brahman, being–consciousness–bliss (Kulārṇava 1.7-8), whose truth is beyond both duality and non-duality (1.110), realised as the bliss of the union of Śakti and Śiva residing in the body (5.79-80).

The body is the temple and the jīva is Sadāśiva; bound by fetters or karma it is jīva, freed it is Sadāśiva — as paddy and husked rice (Kulārṇava 9.41-43); bound by the eight fetters one is a paśu, freed one is Maheśvara (13.90-91).
The body is the temple of the God (Kulārṇava 9.41); the guru knows the unity of the body and the cosmos (13.88).

name: Karma and rebirth in the Kaula view

definitions.definition: Souls covered by ignorance take birth after birth according to merit and demerit in 8.4 million kinds of bodies; the subtle body lasts until liberation; only human birth allows knowledge of reality (Kulārṇava 1.9-17); Kula dharma leads beyond return (2.30).
Human birth is the stairway to liberation, won only by merit; one who wastes it is a self-slayer (Kulārṇava 1.14-17).
The field of human life left fallow could have yielded gold (Rāmprasād).
Verbal knowledge cannot dispel delusion, as talk of a lamp cannot dispel darkness; the truth within is missed by those bewildered in scriptures (Kulārṇava 1.96-100).
Veda, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, Siddhānta, Kaula — each higher than the last, nothing beyond Kaula (Kulārṇava 2.7-8).

name: The three dispositions: paśu, vīra, divya

definitions.definition: The worshipper's disposition determines the mode of worship: paśu (pure, without the Kaula substances), vīra (heroic, with them), divya (divine); the Kālīvilāsa assigns divya to Satya–Tretā, vīra to Tretā–Dvāpara and allows only paśu in the Kali age (4.2-3; 6.10-16); the Buddha's instruction to Vasiṣṭha begins in the paśu disposition (Rudrayāmala 17.137); drinking is threefold by divya, vīra and paśu (Kulārṇava 7.94).

Seven degrees of inner exhilaration in the Kula rite: ārambha, taruṇa, yauvana, prauḍha, tadanta, unmanā and anavastha (Kulārṇava 8.4); the first five are waking, unmanā dream, the equal state deep sleep; knowing them one is liberated (8.94-95).
The Kaula is both enjoyment and yoga; in it enjoyment becomes yoga, sin merit and saṃsāra liberation (Kulārṇava 2.23-24).

name: The Kaula beyond injunction and prohibition

definitions.definition: For the (realized) Kaula there is no injunction or prohibition, merit or sin, heaven or hell (Kulārṇava 9.55-58; 9.62) — yet those who abandon ritual out of false learning go to hell (9.130) and the wilful are condemned (5.96-105).

name: The five tattvas / five M's (pañcatattva, pañca-makāra)

definitions.definition: Wine, meat, fish, parched grain and ritual union, used in the Kaula worship of Śakti (Mahānirvāṇa 5.22-24). Restricted: summary only. The texts bind their use to initiation, consecration and the samayas, and condemn their use for pleasure: wine alone gives no perfection (Kulārṇava 2.117); the uninitiated, wilful or addicted go to hell (5.96-105).
The Kālīvilāsa forbids them in the Kali age, allowing only the paśu disposition (4.2-3).

name: The inner meaning of the Kula substances

definitions.definition: The Kulārṇava gives the rationale: bliss is the form of Brahman residing in the body and the substance manifests it; wine is Śakti, meat Śiva, the enjoyer Bhairava, and the bliss of their union is liberation (5.79-80); those devoted to inner worship are dearest (5.70).
The Tattva circle is truly performed only by those in whom 'all is Brahman' arises (Mahānirvāṇa 8.208); inner worship offers the mind, breath and senses in place of outer substances (5.143-146).

notes: Later yogic readings (e.g. wine as the nectar from the crown, maithuna as the union of Kuṇḍalinī with Śiva) are widespread in Bengal and Nepal commentaries; not anchored here to a specific verse.

name: Substitutes (anukalpa) for the Kaula substances and offerings

definitions.definition: For householders in the Kali age the sweet triad (milk, sugar, honey) replaces wine (Mahānirvāṇa 8.170-171); the last tattva is limited to one's own wife (6.14).
Pumpkin, sugarcane and spirits are 'equal to' an animal victim; coconut water or honey replace wine for the twice-born (Kālikā Purāṇa 67.23; 67.114-115).
Within the circle all castes are twice-born and equal to Śiva — woman, man, eunuch, caṇḍāla or brāhmaṇa; when it ends they are separate again (Kulārṇava 8.96-97). Restricted: summary only.

No caste distinction in giving and drinking within the circle; the Bhairavī circle may be held when occasion arises; the Tattva circle is for those who realise 'all is Brahman' (Mahānirvāṇa 8.151-154; 8.208).

name: Reverence for women in Kaula conduct

definitions.definition: Women are never to be blamed, mocked, insulted or struck — 'not even with a flower' — and their virtues, not faults, proclaimed; every woman is a mother born of the Kula (Kulārṇava 11.61-65); women are goddesses and life-breath (Kaulāvalīnirṇaya 10.87-88).

name: Secrecy and concealment in the Kaula way

definitions.definition: The teaching comes 'from ear to ear' and must not be given to the deceitful (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 6.8-14); reveal the guru but guard the mantra (Kulārṇava 11.88); the Kaulas go 'inwardly Śākta, outwardly Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava in the assembly' (Kaulāvalīnirṇaya 10.94; Kālīvilāsa 7.12); open worship destroys perfection.

name: The guru in the Kaula way

definitions.definition: The guru is father, mother and Maheśvara, and protects when Śiva is angry (Kulārṇava 12.49); rare is the guru who removes suffering rather than wealth (13.104-108); the supreme guru cuts the fetters, gives initiation by piercing and takes up the paśu (13.79), removes the eight fetters and knows the body's lotuses (13.88-94); 'gu' is darkness and 'ru' its remover (17.7).

The guru tests the disciple by knowledge or action for a year, six months or three (Kulārṇava 14.19), and the disciple tests the guru by the bliss and signs of his practice (14.25); if they give and receive without testing both become piśācas (14.11); Kula knowledge never stays in the unworthy (2.36).
Initiation by touch (sparśa), by sight (dṛk) and, rarest, by piercing (vedha) (Kulārṇava 14.53-66).
Kula knowledge shines only for those purified by past merit, devoted to guru and scripture, calm, discreet and obedient (Kulārṇava 2.30-35); the path is harder than walking a sword's edge (2.122).

name: Graded places of worship by eligibility

definitions.definition: God is in fire for brāhmaṇas, in the heart for the wise, in images for the unawakened, everywhere for the knowers of the self (Kulārṇava 9.44).
Without the samaya discipline there is no perfection (Kulārṇava 5.96).
Tāmasa disciples who ignore the samayas and slander the guru become dead while living (Kubjikāmata 12.3-9).

name: The āmnāyas (Kaula transmissions)

definitions.definition: Five āmnāyas from Śiva's five faces — Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern, Upper — the Upper supreme (Kulārṇava 3.7; 3.15-19). In the Kashmir–Nepal scheme reported by scholarship (moderate confidence): the Eastern is the Kula/Trika worship, the Southern Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā), the Western Kubjikā, the Northern Kālī (Krama, Guhyakālī); Nepal adds the Upper and speaks of six (ṣaḍāmnāya).
The Paścimāmnāya is 'the western of all paths' (Kubjikāmata 2.21).

notes: The assignment of goddesses to directions differs between texts; only the Kulārṇava's fivefold list is verse-checked here.

definitions.definition: The Mahākaula passed from Icchā yoginī to the sky-going yoginīs, the Mothers and the earth-going yoginīs; in Kāmarūpa the scripture is in every yoginī's house (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.11-15; 22.10-12).

name: The Siddhas of the Kula (Kaulajñānanirṇaya lists)

definitions.definition: The Kaulajñānanirṇaya names Siddhas who brought down the Kula in the ages, with '-pāda' names (e.g. Vyāghrapāda, Pañcaśikhipāda, Lambodarapāda), and a Goddess's list (Hiḍinipāda, Samudrapāda, Lavaṇapāda, Dhīvarapāda, Siṃhalapāda and others) (9.6-9).

notes: Names read from a corrupt e-text; spellings uncertain.

definitions.definition: The Kulārṇava's last chapter explains terms by their syllables, e.g. guru from 'gu' (darkness) and 'ru' (restraint) (17.7-9).

The avadhūta stage is the saṃnyāsa of the Kali age (Mahānirvāṇa 8.221); avadhūtas are of four kinds, complete (paramahaṃsa) and incomplete; the Śaiva avadhūta is consecrated by the complete consecration (14.142-149).
The vīra avadhūta holds 'I am Śiva, the bliss of Bhairava'; fruits are graded by caste (Nirvāṇa Tantra 14.1-10).

name: The Cīnācāra and the Vasiṣṭha–Buddha story

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: Vasiṣṭha failed to win the Goddess by Vedic austerity and was sent to Mahācīna, where the Buddha taught him the Kula way, beginning with purity, the paśu disposition and breath-yoga (Rudrayāmala 17.105-140); Buddha and Vasiṣṭha are the two Kula-Bhairavas perfected by Ugratārā's mantra (Tārā Tantra 1.2-4).

The Mahāvidyās accomplish for worshippers the acts of killing, driving away, agitation, bewitching, melting, yawning, paralysing and destroying (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.132-133); the six acts (śānti, vaśya, stambhana, vidveṣaṇa, uccāṭana, māraṇa) are treated in the eastern tantras. Recorded only as a teaching; not described. Kṛṣṇānanda treats such claims as needing the tradition's checks.
A mantra held already perfected, needing no checks — said of the Mahāvidyās; Kṛṣṇānanda reads it as praise and keeps the checks (Tantrasāra).
Kālī's mantra is built of seed-syllables (the Karpūrādistotra conceals them in riddles, vv. 1-5); the Mahāvidyā mantras are 'siddha' (Muṇḍamālā). Mantra syllables not reproduced.

Praised as the coiled power of knowledge, will, action and sound, she splits the liṅga and emerges dark and bent (Kubjikāmata 2.2-5), becoming Kubjikā out of shame when asked for the transmission (2.14); her krama-worship enters the Agni Purāṇa (143-144).

relations.note: the hymn describes her as coiled like a sleeping serpent

definitions.definition: 'The western of all paths', given by the Goddess to the Siddhas and spread from Candradvīpa through Śrīśaila, Kiṣkindhā and the western Himalaya (Kubjikāmata 2.20-42).
Where the Kubjikā transmission first descended (Kubjikāmata 1; 2.21).
Where the Kaula scripture came down (Kaulajñānanirṇaya colophons; 22.12).

name: The seats in the Kubjikā tradition

definitions.definition: The Goddess's journey names Śrīśaila, Kiṣkindhā and Oḍḍiyāna (Kubjikāmata 2.23-40); the four seats are levels of the supreme yoni (11.6-7).

name: The sixfold order (ṣaṭprakāra) of the Kubjikā body

definitions.definition: Self, power, haṃsa, breath, channels and body form a sixfold order in which the world is born and which awakens the Kula path (Kubjikāmata 11.13-16); chapters 11-16 set out the six centres with their deities and yoginīs.

After Satī's death Śiva carried her corpse; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śani entered it and dropped its parts across the land; where each fell Śiva stayed as a liṅga and the Goddess is worshipped (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.36-50). Later versions have Viṣṇu cut the body with his discus and count 51 or 52 places.
Uḍḍīyāna (thighs), Kāmarūpa/Kāmagiri (yoni), Jālandhara (breasts), Pūrṇagiri (shoulders and neck), with Devīkūṭa (feet) (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.41-43).
Kāmākhya, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara and Oḍra as the levels beyond form, form, word and body (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7).

name: The Śākta seats (51 / 52 pīṭhas)

definitions.definition: The seats where parts of Satī fell, each with its goddess and guardian Bhairava; the Kālikā Purāṇa knows a small set (18.41-50); the late Pīṭhanirṇaya lists 51 (Bengali lists 51 or 52, with upapīṭhas); other texts count 108.

notes: The 51-pīṭha list is not reproduced: it was not checked against the Pīṭhanirṇaya text in Phase B (see REPORT).

definitions.definition: The Goddess of the yoni-pīṭha at Kāmagiri in Kāmarūpa (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42, 18.49), 'the great vidyā in the form of the yoni' who is all four aims of life (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4, 1.9-13). The temple on Nīlācala was rebuilt by the Koch king Naranārāyaṇa in 1565 (historical metadata, moderate confidence).
Seat of the Kaula scripture and yoginīs (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 22.10-12).

name: Ambubachi: the Goddess's annual menstruation

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: during the three days of ambuvācī in Āṣāḍha the Earth menstruates; at Kāmākhyā the Goddess herself is in her courses, the temple is closed, and on the fourth day it reopens and pieces of red cloth are given as prasāda (the Ambubachi Melā). A Bengali ritual calendar in the Prāṇatoṣiṇī names 'ambuvācī, three days'.

notes: Living temple practice; no scriptural verse anchoring the Kāmākhyā menstruation was checked in Phase B.

definitions.definition: The Goddess's yoni fallen at Kāmagiri is the chief seat (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42); Kāmākhyā is the great vidyā in the form of the yoni (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4); the Yoni Tantra teaches its worship (restricted, summary only).
The supreme is the primal yoni, fourfold (Kubjikāmata 11.6).

name: Menstruation as sacred in Śākta rites

definitions.definition: The Goddess's menstruation is honoured at Kāmākhyā (Ambubachi); some late Kaula tantras treat menstrual blood ('self-born flower') as a sacred substance (restricted, named only).

name: The sixty-four yoginīs and their temples

definitions.definition: A circle of sixty-four yoginī goddesses worshipped in open-roofed circular temples of c. 9th–11th c. — Hirapur and Ranipur-Jharial (Odisha), Bheraghat near Jabalpur, Mitaoli (Morena), Khajuraho (rectangular) and others; the yoginīs are the Kula's transmitters (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.11-15). Their name-lists differ widely between texts.

notes: Temple locations and dates are historical metadata (moderate confidence); the yoginī name-lists are not reproduced.

definitions.definition: The Kālikā Purāṇa teaches offering animals to the Goddess, says it brings heaven, liberation and victory, allows substitutes and forbids brāhmaṇas certain offerings and wine (67.1-12; 67.19-23; 67.46-52; 67.113-117). Restricted: summary only. Practised at Kāmākhyā and in Bengal; opposed by Vaiṣṇava and many Śākta dakṣiṇa worshippers.
Worship of a young girl as the Goddess — in the eastern tantras and in the Bengal Durgā-pūjā; the Kulārṇava forbids insulting a maiden or girl (11.61).

name: Śyāmā-saṅgīt: devotion to the Mother in song

definitions.definition: The Bengali Śākta songs of Rāmprasād and Kamalākānta address Kālī as Mother with intimacy — pleading, reproaching, claiming the child's right, using her name as protection, and seeing the world as her play; they draw on tantric imagery (the six centres, the cremation ground) but make devotion the path.
The devotee's affectionate complaint that the Mother keeps her child turning like the blindfolded oil-press ox (Rāmprasād).

name: The world as the Mother's play

definitions.definition: The Mother dances, sings and keeps time by herself (song ascribed to Kamalākānta).
The abode of Śiva in the crown is called Brahman by some, Viṣṇu's state by others, Haṃsa by others (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 50); the commentary: the final goal of Śaivas, Śāktas and Vaiṣṇavas alike.

Śākta view (Pūrṇānanda): the Goddess herself, coiled three and a half times round the Svayambhū liṅga, is led up through the centres to unite with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus, the bliss of which is liberation (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 51-53).
Kubjikā is praised as coiled like a sleeping serpent (Kubjikāmata 2.2).
